title: Multi-Candidate Ballot Problem
description: Generalizes the classical Ballot Problem from 2 candidates to m candidates. Proves the reduction principle: P(candidate 0 leads all opponents combined throughout counting) = (a-b)/(a+b), exactly the classical formula. Uses projection to 2-candidate sequences, fiber uniformity, and connects to Mathlib's Wiedijk #30. 498 lines, 20 theorems, 0 axioms, 0 sorries.

overview.historicalContext:
**Multi-Candidate Ballot Problem**

Bertrand (1887) proved the classical ballot theorem: if candidate A receives a votes and candidate B receives b votes with a > b, the probability A leads throughout the counting is (a-b)/(a+b). This file extends the result to m ≥ 2 candidates, proving that the "leads all opponents combined" probability is identical to the 2-candidate formula.
overview.problemStatement: **Theorem (Reduction Principle)**: Given m candidates where candidate 0 receives a votes and all others combined receive b votes (a > b), the probability candidate 0 leads all opponents combined throughout equals (a-b)/(a+b) — exactly the classical 2-candidate ballot formula.
overview.proofStrategy:
The proof has three key steps:

1. **Projection**: Map m-candidate vote sequences to 2-candidate (±1) sequences by collapsing all non-zero candidates to -1
2. **Prefix sum preservation**: The projection preserves the "leads throughout" property because prefix sums only depend on votes-for vs votes-against
3. **Fiber uniformity**: Every 2-candidate pattern has the same number of m-candidate refinements (b!/(a₁!·...·aₘ₋₁!)), so conditional probability equals the classical result
keyInsights: The 'leads all combined' property depends only on which positions have a vote for candidate 0 vs against
Fiber uniformity: each binary pattern has b!/(a₁!·...·aₘ₋₁!) multi-candidate refinements
The reduction makes the m-candidate problem no harder than the 2-candidate case

sections.title: Part I: Projection from Multi-Candidate to 2-Candidate
sections.summary: Defines the projection map from m-candidate vote sequences to ±1 sequences: vote for candidate 0 maps to +1, all others to -1.

sections.title: Part II: Prefix Sums and Leading Property
sections.summary: Defines prefix sums and the 'leads throughout' predicate. Proves prefix sum preservation under projection.

sections.title: Part III: Projection Preserves Leading
sections.summary: Proves the key equivalence: candidate 0 leads all opponents combined iff the projected ±1 sequence has all positive prefix sums.

sections.title: Part IV: Concrete Instantiation with Fin m
sections.summary: Instantiates the abstract framework with Fin m for concrete computations.

sections.title: Part V: Connection to Mathlib's Ballot Theorem
sections.summary: Links the projected sequences to Mathlib's countedSequence type, enabling use of the classical ballot theorem.

sections.title: Part VII: Fiber Uniformity
sections.summary: The core counting argument: all projected patterns have equal preimage sizes under the projection map, proving the conditional probability equals the classical formula.

sections.title: Parts VIII-IX: Examples and Open Challenge
sections.summary: Conditional probability framework, concrete verification examples, and statement of the harder 'full ordering' problem (candidate 0 leads each individual opponent).

conclusion.summary: A complete proof (0 sorries, 0 axioms) that the multi-candidate ballot problem reduces to the classical 2-candidate case. The fiber uniformity argument shows the reduction is exact, not approximate.
conclusion.implications:
**Significance**

1. **Clean generalization**: Extends Wiedijk #30 to arbitrary numbers of candidates with zero axioms.
2. **Connects to Mathlib**: Directly uses Archive.Wiedijk100Theorems.BallotProblem.
3. **Fiber counting technique**: The uniform fiber argument is a general technique applicable to other combinatorial probability problems.
openQuestions: Can the 'full ordering' problem (candidate 0 leads each individual opponent) be solved using similar projection techniques?
What is the probability of a specific ranking order among all m candidates?
